sections.markdown:
## C — Helping teens and new drivers learn: setting the example, permit and supervised hours, attitude, talking through drives, planning practice in four phases, coaching habits, driving logs and contracts, non-English speakers and continued monitoring
Knowledge domain: how a parent or mentor helps a new Tennessee driver learn — why your own driving is the first lesson, what the permit and supervised-hours rules require, why attitude matters, how to teach out loud, how to plan practice from a parking lot to the interstate, how to coach calmly, how logs and family driving agreements help, how to help non-English speakers, and why supervision continues after the license.

FACT_ID: sec17-F01 | anchor: A01
The most important thing you can do when teaching someone to drive is to drive safely yourself, because the new driver copies your habits. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F02 | anchor: A01
Examiners often hear young drivers defend habits such as rolling stops by saying that is how their parent drives. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F03 | anchor: A01
People under 18 must hold a learner permit for 180 days and qualify under the graduated license program before they can take the road test. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F04 | anchor: A01
Attitude decides whether a new driver will cooperate or compete in traffic and whether the driver accepts high risk or practices defensive driving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F05 | anchor: A01
A mentor's patience, courtesy and willingness to improve are the best assets, and setting that example may do more than anything else for a teen's safety. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F06 | anchor: A01
Talking out loud while you drive, about tricky signs, yellow-light decisions, surrounding traffic and the two-second rule, uses teachable moments without overloading the learner. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F07 | anchor: A01
Plan every practice session in advance, because aimless driving can be dangerous for a novice, especially early on. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F08 | anchor: A01
Before practicing in traffic, make sure the learner has good hand and foot coordination, since a novice unsure of the pedals may hit the wrong one in a panic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F09 | anchor: A01
In phase one, practice basic car control somewhere safe and away from traffic, and a large empty parking lot is ideal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F10 | anchor: A01
Phase one skills include buckling up, adjusting the seat and mirrors, using the gearshift and pedals, backing up, pulling forward, turning and staying within an imaginary lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec17-F11 | anchor: A02
In phase two, in a quiet residential area, add pulling into traffic, simple intersections, lane position with a two-second following gap, and easy lane changes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F12 | anchor: A02
In phase three, once basic control is mastered, move to heavier traffic and add parallel and hill parking, multiple-turn-lane intersections, U-turns and quick stops. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F13 | anchor: A02
In phase four, practice everything on high-speed highways or interstates, in different weather, at night in good and bad weather, and in city or heavy traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F14 | anchor: A02
Give directions well ahead of time and use the same words every time, such as always saying gas pedal rather than switching to accelerator. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F15 | anchor: A02
Do not yell and fuss over every mistake; respond calmly, because criticism can quickly erode a new driver's confidence. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F16 | anchor: A02
After a major mistake, stop as soon as you safely can while it is fresh, and discuss what happened and what the safest response would have been. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F17 | anchor: A02
Researchers find that the more supervised miles new drivers log before driving alone, the fewer crashes they have. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F18 | anchor: A02
Tennessee's graduated license program requires minors to drive 50 hours before they can move up to the intermediate license. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F19 | anchor: A02
In their first year of driving, about one in five 16-year-old male drivers and about one in ten 16-year-old female drivers will have a crash. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F20 | anchor: A02
Some of the worst teen crashes happen at night and with a group of young people in the car, which is why the graduated license program restricts both. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F21 | anchor: A02
A beginner's worst enemy is overconfidence after quickly learning the basics, so skill-building must continue after the license. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec17-F22 | anchor: A03
Every applicant must understand and speak enough English to communicate safely with the examiner before a road test can be given. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]

FACT_ID: sec17-F23 | anchor: A03
A license examiner rides with your child for less than 30 minutes, and passing that test does not guarantee safe habits afterward. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]

FACT_ID: sec17-F24 | anchor: A03
The examiner judges competence, but teaching the child to drive is the parent's or mentor's responsibility, so keep monitoring a teen's driving after licensing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0132]

Misconceptions: the road test is not proof that safe habits will last; random practice drives are not harmless; correcting every mistake loudly does not speed learning; early success is a reason for continued practice, not for relaxing.
Mnemonics: lot, neighborhood, traffic, highway for the four practice phases; same words, said early; stop and discuss while it is fresh.
Glossary: graduated driver license program means Tennessee's staged licensing system for drivers under eighteen; teachable moment means a real driving situation used to explain a skill; driving log means a record of supervised practice; driving contract means a family agreement on when, where and how a teen may drive.
Dynamic facts: the permit holding period, the supervised hours requirement and the teen crash rates are set by Tennessee law or come from dated research; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
